passage: Two hours before the application portal closed, Varun sat on a delayed train with his phone at fifteen per cent and one bar of signal, polishing his public profile. He had typed "visionary leader" and "award-winning" over a college quiz he had co-won. His sister Shreya called. "Why do you sound like a brochure?" Varun laughed, uneasy. He read it back and felt like an actor. He cut the puffed-up words and wrote what he had actually done: led a four-person project, co-won a state quiz. He kept the good photo. The cooking pictures stayed in the private account that only close friends could see. He submitted with a minute to spare.

qa.q: What did Shreya ask when she called?
qa.a: Shreya asked, Why do you sound like a brochure?

qa.q: How did Varun feel reading the profile back, and why?
qa.a: Like an actor; uneasy because the puffed-up words were not what Varun had actually done.

qa.q: Which choices kept the profile honest but still polished?
qa.a: Cutting the inflated words, stating what Varun had actually done and keeping the cooking pictures private.

qa.q: Why might Shreya have made the brochure remark?
qa.a: Shreya heard that the profile did not sound like Varun and joked gently to nudge honesty.

grounding: A young professional curates a public image, feels the strain of performing, and stays honest while keeping private space.

passage: In the Kolkata office lift, Yusuf overheard Arnab muttering a caption. "Led the whole campaign," it said. Arnab had actually built one of three parts. Every evening Arnab posted a polished update, and lately the effort felt like a second job: checking reactions before dinner and going to bed feeling flat. Yusuf said lightly, "You're better than your captions." Arnab thought about that all the way home. That night the caption became "Built the email part of a team campaign," and the post got fewer likes. Arnab felt lighter anyway. The weekend photos moved to a separate account with just a few close friends.

qa.q: How many parts of the campaign had Arnab actually built?
qa.a: Arnab had built one of three parts.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel about the daily posting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Arnab felt drained and weary; the effort felt like a second job and Arnab went to bed feeling flat.

qa.q: Which changes kept Arnab's image honest and protected privacy?
qa.a: Rewriting the caption to say exactly what Arnab did and moving weekend photos to a separate account for close friends.

qa.q: What might Yusuf have meant by You're better than your captions?
qa.a: That Arnab's real work was good enough and did not need exaggeration, said kindly and briefly.

grounding: A young professional curates a public image, feels the strain, and returns to honest captions and a private circle.

passage:
"Can you read this before I post it?" Ankita turned her laptop to Lokesh.
"'Thrilled to share that every day at the agency is a new adventure. Grateful for this incredible team.' Ankita, you cried in the bathroom yesterday."
"That's not the point. Recruiters look at the profile."
"I know. But 'every day is a new adventure'?"
"Everyone writes like that." She rubbed her eyes. "Honestly, I'm tired. I spend Sunday planning posts. I smile in every photo. I feel like a brochure."
"Then write something true but still professional. What did you actually learn?"
She thought. "How to handle a client who changes the brief five times."
"Post that. People would read that."
"And the crying?"
"Keep that for me and your sister. Not everything goes online."
Ankita deleted the first line. Her shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: What did Ankita actually learn at work?
qa.a: How to handle a client who changes the brief five times.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel about keeping up her online image?
qa.a: Ankita feels tired and strained, spending Sundays planning posts and feeling like a brochure.

qa.q: What advice did Lokesh give, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: He suggested posting something true but professional and keeping private struggles for close people, so the profile stays honest without exposing everything.

qa.q: What would change if Ankita posted the 'new adventure' line after all?
qa.a: It would add to the gap between her public image and real life, and the strain of performing would probably grow.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who curates an image for work and followers, feels the strain, and chooses honest posts while keeping some things private.

passage:
Two years ago I started posting my home cooking to get noticed, and it worked a little: four thousand followers, a small brand of spices asking for a collaboration I turned down. What nobody saw was the other side. I, Nitin, would cook a dish three times to get the steam right in the photo. I ate cold dinners. I wrote cheerful captions on days I felt flat. Once my friend Aditi dropped by and I asked her to stand still while I shot her plate. She put her fork down and said, "Are we eating or filming?" That stung, because it was true.
So I changed a few things. I still post, but once a week, and only food I actually cooked for people. I made a second, locked account for eleven friends, where I post burnt rotis. Aditi follows both. She says the second one is funnier.

qa.q: How many friends can see the second, locked account?
qa.a: Eleven friends.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when Aditi asked "Are we eating or filming?"
qa.a: Nitin felt stung and a little ashamed, because the question was true.

qa.q: Which changes helped Nitin, and why?
qa.a: Posting once a week only food cooked for people, and keeping a locked account for friends, kept the public page honest and gave Nitin a private space.

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi when she had to wait for the photo?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt frustrated and a bit hurt, as if the visit mattered less than the post.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who curates a public cooking image, feels the strain of performing, and protects honesty and a private space.

passage:
Supervisor's note, design studio, Friday.
For three weeks Parul has been posting her work every morning on the portfolio site and on two social accounts, each piece with a long caption about "passion". She is good, and the posts are getting her noticed; two recruiters wrote to her. But I noticed she comes in with red eyes, redoes screenshots of the same mock-up four times, and checks follower counts during reviews. On Tuesday she said, half joking, "I have to be the brand now, not a person."
I asked her to lunch today. I said some curation is part of the job, and I do it too. I also said her best piece this year was one she never posted, because it was private work for a small bakery. We agreed she would post twice a week, keep weekends offline, and let Jagdish from the team review captions for honesty, not polish.
Supervisor, P. Nair

qa.q: How many recruiters wrote to Parul?
qa.a: Two recruiters wrote to her.

qa.q: What did Parul's comment "I have to be the brand now, not a person" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt strained and pressured, as if performing online had taken over who she was.

qa.q: What plan did they agree on, and what makes it balanced?
qa.a: Posting twice a week, weekends offline and a teammate reviewing captions for honesty; it keeps some curation for jobs while protecting rest and truth.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see the task of reviewing captions?
qa.a: Jagdish might feel trusted and glad to help Parul sound like herself, while perhaps unsure how blunt to be about honesty.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who curates her public image and feels the strain, and a supervisor who helps her keep it honest with private time.

passage:
Aditi's journal, Sunday night.
Posted my "lessons from my first year as a product manager" slides today. Lots of likes, two recruiters in my inbox. I should feel great.
I don't, fully. Lesson 4 was "embrace failure", with a photo of me smiling at my desk. The actual failure was the launch in March, when I cried in the office bathroom. Nobody sees that version.
Every weekend now I think about what would make a good post instead of just living the weekend.
Lalit came over for dinner and said, "You told me more tonight than your whole page ever has." He meant it kindly. It stung anyway.
Decisions: I'll keep posting, it helps with work. But only true things, no fake glow. And the Sunday trek group, the dal I burn, Nani's calls: those stay off the internet. Some of me should just be mine.

qa.q: What was Lesson 4 in Aditi's post?
qa.a: Lesson 4 was "embrace failure".

qa.q: Why doesn't Aditi feel fully great about the likes?
qa.a: Aditi feels uneasy and a bit fake, because the smiling photo hides the day she cried in the office bathroom.

qa.q: What balance does Aditi decide on?
qa.a: Aditi will keep posting for work but only true things, and keep private parts of life, like the trek group and Nani's calls, off the internet.

qa.q: What might Lalit have meant by his comment at dinner?
qa.a: Lalit likely felt close to Aditi and wanted to gently point out that the real Aditi shows up in person, not on the page.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who curates a public image, feels the strain of performing, and chooses honesty and private spaces to protect the self.
